messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 35
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: UX Designer
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 73

He is a 35-year-old South Eastern Asian man who comes to therapy after surviving a life-threatening illness that, in his words, “came out of nowhere and turned my life into a waiting room.” Before the illness, he describes himself as steady, practical, and exacting in the way he approaches his work as a UX designer. He likes clean lines, clear logic, and problems that can be improved if he studies them closely enough. His days used to be organized around screen work, design reviews, and long conversations with a small team about how to make something feel more intuitive for the people using it. He says he took pride in making other people’s experiences easier, even while his own life felt busy and ordinary.

Then he becomes sick. He remembers the first signs as vague and easy to dismiss: fatigue, a heaviness in his body, a sense that something was “off” but not yet serious. He keeps working at first, telling himself it is stress or poor sleep. The illness sharpens quickly. Medical appointments multiply, tests come back abnormal, and soon he is hearing words he cannot fully absorb. He describes sitting in exam rooms trying to understand doctors through a fog of fear, nodding even when he cannot track what is being said. He remembers the sudden shift from being a person with plans to being a person whose life depends on blood draws, scans, and the competence of strangers. What unsettles him most is how fast control disappears. He says he has always assumed that if he stayed informed and prepared, he could prevent disaster. In the hospital, that belief collapses.

During the worst period, he feels his body become unreliable in a way that frightens him more than the illness itself. He notices every sensation and immediately wonders if it means he is deteriorating. He cannot sleep well, partly because of pain and medication effects, and partly because his mind will not let him rest. At night he lies awake replaying conversations with doctors, searching for omissions or hidden meanings. He becomes hypervigilant to his own body, checking for changes in breathing, pulse, temperature, and fatigue. He starts to associate ordinary bodily sensations with danger. A cough, a twinge, an odd flutter in his chest can send him spiraling into panic.

His wife becomes his anchor, but he also notices how frightened she is, and that fright deepens his own. He says one of the hardest parts is seeing concern on the faces of the people he loves and not being able to reassure them. In their home, which once felt private and predictable, everything begins to carry the atmosphere of illness. Pill bottles appear on the counter. Conversations become careful. He feels guilty for the burden he places on his wife and for the way the illness interrupts the life they had expected to build together. Even after the most acute phase passes, he does not feel relieved in the way he expects. Instead, he feels altered, as if something essential has been broken and then hastily stitched back together.

When he returns to work, he finds that his old concentration does not come easily. He can still do the job, but the ease is gone. Tasks that once felt straightforward now require more effort because his attention keeps sliding toward internal alarms. In meetings, he sometimes loses track of what is being said because he is monitoring his body or scanning for signs that he is becoming ill again. He worries that colleagues can tell he is not fully present. As a designer, he is accustomed to noticing what is broken in a system, yet now that sensitivity turns inward and becomes exhausting. He tries to regain control by overplanning, double-checking medical information, and researching symptoms late into the night, but the more he looks, the more threatened he feels.

He also experiences unwanted memories of the hospital that arrive with the force of relived fear. Certain smells, the beeping sound of monitors, or even the sterile brightness of a clinic waiting room can pull him back into the period when he believed he might die. He does not describe these reactions dramatically; instead, he speaks about them with embarrassment, as though he should have moved on by now. He avoids hospitals when he can and feels tense every time he has a follow-up appointment. Even when the results are reassuring, he cannot fully trust them. The relief never lasts long before his mind asks what comes next.

Over time, his world narrows. He becomes more cautious about travel, more protective of routines, and more reluctant to make plans far ahead. He says he feels divided between the part of him that wants to return to normal and the part that no longer believes normal is safe. Still, he keeps showing up—to work, to appointments, to marriage, to the life he has not entirely lost. Beneath his guardedness, there is grief for the version of himself who moved through the world with less fear, and there is also a stubborn wish to feel at home in his own body again.
